All numbers, tables and figures below were produced by the analysis run named above and are stored with it.

Summary

Kidney cancer multi-omics: RNA + methylation + mutations (TCGA-KIRC) was analysed with the Multi-omics integration workflow (version 1.0.0) on the LSMA Analysis Lab. To describe how the samples group by 'vital_status'. In summary, 6 shared factors were found; 2 groups of patients were found; the model was wrong for 28% of held-out samples. 4 point(s) are flagged under Limitations and should be read before the results are used.

  • 6 shared factors were found.
  • 2 groups of patients were found.
  • The model was wrong for 28% of held-out samples.

Introduction

Several kinds of measurement on the same patients (for example expression, methylation, mutations and protein) analysed together: how far the layers agree, which features are linked across layers, the hidden factors they share (MOFA), groups of patients found from all layers at once (similarity network fusion) and a model that tells known groups apart using every layer (DIABLO). The data analysed here is of kind 'multi_omics'.

Aim

To describe how the samples group by 'vital_status'.

Methods

Assembled from what each completed stage recorded. Check it against the parameter tables below before using it in a write-up.

3 layers measured on the same 100 patients were analysed together (expression: 2,000 continuous features; methylation: 2,000 continuous features; mutations: 32 binary features). Features were kept as follows: continuous layers: at most 2,000 most variable features without missing values; yes/no layers: features present in at least 5 and absent in at least 5 patients.

Agreement between layers was measured with the Mantel test on Euclidean distances between patients (standardised features, Spearman correlation, permutation p-values): expression and methylation r = 0.529; expression and mutations r = 0.069; methylation and mutations r = 0.041.

Links between features of different layers: Spearman correlation between continuous layers; Wilcoxon rank-sum test between a yes/no layer and a continuous layer; Benjamini-Hochberg correction within each pair of layers; screened were the 100 most variable features of each continuous layer; the 30 most frequent of each yes/no layer; pairs with adjusted p-value below 0.05 were called.

Shared factors were estimated with MOFA2 (expression: continuous, each feature standardised; methylation: continuous, each feature standardised; mutations: yes/no); 6 factors explaining at least 1% of the variance of a layer were kept.

Patients were grouped with similarity network fusion (SNFtool; 20 neighbours, sigma 0.5, 20 iterations) and spectral clustering; the number of groups (2) was chosen by the eigengap rule.

Several ways of grouping the patients were compared at 2 groups each (expression alone, methylation alone, mutations alone, All layers pasted together, Similarity network fusion, Shared factors (MOFA), Generalised canonical correlation), including simple concatenation of the layers as a baseline. Groupings were compared with each other and with the column 'vital_status' using the adjusted Rand index.

A supervised multi-layer model for 'vital_status' was fitted with DIABLO (mixOmics block.splsda), 2 components, 15 features per layer and component, link between layers 0.1 and assessed by 5-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times, weighted vote of the layers, centroid distance: balanced error rate 0.281 (guessing: 0.5; median with shuffled labels: 0.485; permutation p = 0.02).

Random seed: 42. Software: R 4.5.2; Bioconductor 3.21; MOFA2 1.18.0; SNFtool 2.3.1; cluster 2.1.8.1; data.table 1.18.6.1; jsonlite 2.0.0; mixOmics 6.32.0; mofapy2 0.7.5; reticulate 1.47.0; survival 3.8.3.

Analyses were run on the LSMA Analysis Lab (workflow 'multi-omics' version 1.0.0).

Stage 2 of 7

Each layer and their agreement Exploratory

Every layer gets its own principal component analysis. Then the layers are compared in pairs: for each pair, the distances between all pairs of patients in one layer are correlated with their distances in the other (a Mantel test, with a permutation p-value).

Key numbers

Layersexpression, methylation, mutations
Coloured bystage
Lowest agreement0.041
Highest agreement0.529

What this stage found

This stage recorded lowest agreement: 0.041 and highest agreement: 0.529.

This is shown in Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 5 and Figure 6.

How to interpret this stage

In the demonstration data, messenger RNA separates the basal tumours sharply. Messenger RNA and microRNA agree fairly well about the patients (a Mantel correlation of about 0.6); protein agrees much less with either (0.2 to 0.3). Values near 1 would mean a layer adds nothing new; values near 0 mean the layers have little in common.

Parameters used

ParameterValue
Colour the patients by (color_by)stagechanged from default
Permutations for the agreement test (permutations)499default

Stage 3 of 7

Links between layers Statistically supported

For each pair of layers, features are tested against each other across the patients. Two continuous features (a gene's expression and a protein's abundance) are compared with the Spearman correlation. A yes/no feature (a mutated gene) and a continuous one are compared with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. P-values are corrected for all the pairs tested. Where the same name appears in two layers, such as a gene measured as mRNA and as protein, the correlation of the two is reported for every such feature.

Stage 4 of 7

Shared factors (MOFA) Exploratory

Multi-omics factor analysis (MOFA) is a generalisation of principal component analysis to several layers. It looks for a small number of hidden factors, each a pattern across the patients, and reports for every factor how much of the variation of each layer it explains. A factor can be shared by several layers or belong to one. Each factor comes with weights that say which features carry it.

What this stage found

This stage recorded number of factors: 6, number of factors shared between layers: 5 and dropped factors below percent: 1.

This is shown in Figure 11, Figure 12, Figure 13, Figure 14, Figure 15, Figure 16 and Figure 17.

How to interpret this stage

Read the variance heatmap first: which factors are shared? Then colour the patients by the sample-sheet columns and look at the table of associations. In the demonstration data the first factor is active in all three layers and separates the basal tumours from the others; it was found without being told the subtype. Then read the features with the largest weights.

Stage 5 of 7

Patient groups (SNF) Exploratory

Similarity network fusion (SNF) builds, for each layer, a network in which two patients are connected strongly when they are alike in that layer. The networks then exchange information step by step until they converge to one fused network: connections supported by several layers are strengthened, those seen in one layer only fade. The patients are grouped on the fused network by spectral clustering.

Note. The mean silhouette width is 0.05: the patients do not fall into clearly separate groups. Read the grouping as one way of cutting a continuum.
Note. The fused groups are almost the groups of the layer 'expression' alone; the other layers contribute little.

This stage recorded number of patients: 100, number of groups: 2, mean silhouette width: 0.047 and survival log rank p: 0.000582.

This is shown in Figure 18, Figure 19, Figure 20, Figure 21, Figure 22 and Figure 23.

The stage raised 2 warnings, given in full below.

How to interpret this stage

Look at the fused similarity heatmap for blocks, at the bar chart to see whether one layer alone decides the groups, and at the table that relates the groups to the sample sheet. In the demonstration data two groups are proposed without any label: one holds nearly all basal tumours and some Her2 tumours, the other all luminal A tumours and the remaining Her2 ones. The bar chart shows that messenger RNA alone gives almost the same groups and protein contributes next to nothing, which is worth knowing before calling the result "multi-omic". Ask for three groups and see whether Her2 separates.

Stage 6 of 7

Telling groups apart (DIABLO) Statistically supported

DIABLO builds, for each layer, a component from a small number of features such that the components separate the known groups and are correlated with each other across layers. The result is a multi-layer signature. Its error is estimated by repeated cross-validation: patients are held out, the features are chosen again from the others, and the held-out patients are classified. The whole procedure is repeated with shuffled group labels to show what chance looks like.

Stage 7 of 7

Methods compared Statistically supported

The patients are grouped several different ways and the groupings are set side by side. Each layer alone; all layers simply pasted together after scaling, which is the naive approach; similarity network fusion; the shared factors from MOFA, if that stage was run; and generalised canonical correlation. Every method is asked for the same number of groups. The groupings are then compared with each other, and with a column of the sample sheet that none of them was given.

Note. One layer on its own ('expression') recovers 'vital_status' as well as every method that combines them. The other layers are adding nothing to this grouping.
Note. Some methods agree barely more than chance with each other. A grouping that only one method finds should not be reported as a subtype without evidence from outside this dataset.

The stage raised 2 warnings, given in full below.

How to interpret this stage

Read the heatmap first. Methods that agree with each other are finding the same structure, whatever their machinery. Then read the bar chart against the known column, and compare every integration method with the bar for pasting the layers together. If that bar is as tall as the others, the integration earned nothing on this data, and the stage says so.

Discussion

What the run amounts to, drawn from the stages that carry a judgement. Every sentence below was written by the stage that reached it; none is a later interpretation.

This run describes the data rather than testing a hypothesis about it, so there is no verdict to draw together here. The Results describe what was measured.

The run raised 4 warnings, listed with the stages that raised them. They are part of the result, not notes beside it.

Everything above was produced by Multi-omics integration on the data named in the Data section, with the parameters recorded under each stage. The Limitations section says what this design cannot show, and should be read before any of this is quoted.
